t.2.30.1: Having given much wealth to the brāhmaṇas together with Vaidehī, the two Rāghavas went with Sītā to see their father.
t.2.30.2: Then the two weapons, taken up and dreadful to behold, shone forth, hung with strands of garlands and adorned by Sītā.
t.2.30.3: Then the splendid people, having climbed onto the palaces and mansions and the summits of the towering buildings, looked on, listless and dejected.
t.2.30.4: For the streets, thronged with many people, could not be traversed; therefore, climbing onto the mansions, the people, downcast, gazed upon Rāghava.
t.2.30.5: Then, seeing Rāma on foot and without a parasol, the people, their minds stricken with grief, spoke words of many kinds.
t.2.30.6: He whom, as he went forth, a great fourfold army used to follow, him, now alone, Lakṣmaṇa follows together with Sītā.
t.2.30.7: Though he knows the savor of sovereignty and grants the desires of those who seek them, out of reverence for dharma he does not wish to make his father untruthful.
t.2.30.8: She who could not formerly be seen even by beings moving through the sky, that Sītā the people standing on the royal road now behold today.
t.2.30.9: Rain, heat and cold will swiftly bring pallor to Sītā, who is used to fragrant body-unguents and accustomed to red sandalwood paste.
t.2.30.11: How could there be banishment even of a son devoid of virtues? How much less of one by whom this whole world has been won through his conduct alone!
t.2.30.10: Surely Daśaratha speaks today as one possessed by some spirit, for a king ought not to banish his beloved son.
t.2.30.12: Kindness, compassion, learning, good character, self-restraint and tranquility of mind: these six virtues adorn Rāghava, the best of men.
t.2.30.13: Therefore, through the harm done to him, the people are sorely afflicted, like water-dwelling creatures in the hot season from the drying up of the water.
t.2.30.14: Through the suffering of this lord of the world, the whole world is afflicted, just as a tree laden with flowers and fruit is afflicted by an injury to its root.
t.2.30.16: Abandoning our gardens, our fields and our houses, let us follow the righteous Rāma, sharing with him one and the same sorrow and joy.
t.2.30.15: Like Lakṣmaṇa, we too, with our wives and our kinsmen, shall swiftly follow him as he goes, taking the road by which Rāghava goes.
t.2.30.17: …houses whose buried treasures have been dug up and whose courtyards lie in ruins, whose wealth and grain have been taken away, and whose valuables have been carried off entirely.
t.2.30.19: Let the forest to which Rāghava goes become a city, and let the city, abandoned by us, become a forest.
t.2.30.18: Let Kaikeyī take possession of these dwellings, strewn with dust, forsaken by the deities and abandoned by us.
t.2.30.21: Thus did Rāma hear these various words spoken by many different people, and having heard them, his mind was not disturbed.
t.2.30.20: Let all the fanged beasts from their lairs, and the deer and birds from the mountain ridges, take over what we have abandoned, and let them abandon the places we shall now inhabit.
t.2.30.22: Then Rāma, looking upon his kinsfolk who were stricken with grief, himself showing no sign of distress and seeming almost to smile, went forth eager to see his father, wishing to carry out his father's command as was proper.
t.2.30.23: Then the great-souled Rāma, son of the Ikṣvāku line, about to depart for the forest, first beheld that scene of distress; and, seeing Sumantra, the great-souled one stood waiting so that he might be announced to his father.
t.2.30.24: Then Rāghava, devoted to dharma, having firmly resolved by his father's command to enter the forest, looked at Sumantra and said, "Announce my coming to the king."
